intro: Every person starts life in a particular place, a particular family and a particular language. Some start with more money, some with less. Some grow up speaking the language of their grandparents, and some grow up between two languages. This unit looks at the world today and asks how much those starting points shape a life, and how people move beyond them.

In the first chapter you will learn how economists measure gaps between rich and poor, and how easily children move up or down compared with their parents. You will compare Norway, Brazil, Britain, India and China. In the second chapter you will follow music, food and people across borders. You will study how countries welcome newcomers and how communities keep languages alive. Then you will walk through four Chicago neighborhoods.

By the end, you will be able to read a Gini score and a mobility chart and explain what they show. You will be able to describe the main views on inequality and migration fairly. You will also be able to use evidence to argue your own answer to the unit's big question.
bigQuestion: How much do birth, class and culture shape who we become, and how do people and societies change them?

title: Class and Culture Today

chapters.title: Inequality and Social Mobility
chapters.bigQuestion: How much does the place and family you are born into shape the life you can build?

story.title: Two Babies, One Birthday
story.kicker: A student follows two newborns, one in Oslo and one in São Paulo, and asks what their chances really are.
paragraphs: Mariana is in tenth grade, and her project starts with a simple idea. Picture two babies born on the same morning. One is born in a hospital in Oslo, the capital of Norway. The other is born in a hospital in São Paulo, the largest city in Brazil. Both are healthy. Both have parents who love them. Mariana wants to know what the numbers say about the lives ahead of them.

She starts with money. Norway is one of the most equal countries in the world, measured by how income is shared. Brazil is one of the most unequal. In São Paulo, glass towers with rooftop helicopter pads stand a short drive from crowded hillside neighborhoods called favelas. In Oslo, the gap between a bus driver's pay and a lawyer's pay is smaller than in most countries.

Next she looks at schools and health. Both babies can go to free public schools. But in Brazil, many families who can afford it pay for private schools, and the public schools vary a great deal. In Norway, almost every child goes to the same kind of public school. Mariana notices that the Oslo baby's future seems to depend less on which family she was born into.

Then Mariana finds a surprise. Some economists argue that countries with bigger gaps between rich and poor also have less movement between generations. In those places, children tend to stay near where their parents started. Other economists question how strong that link is. Mariana realizes her project is really about one question: how much of a life is set at birth, and how much can a person change?
story.think: What would you want to know about a country to guess how much a baby born there could move up in life?

lessons.title: Income Versus Wealth
lessons.mainIdea: Income is money coming in over time, while wealth is what a person owns minus what they owe, and wealth is usually far more unequal.
reading: Think about two neighbors. Ana earns $80,000 a year as a nurse, but she rents her apartment and still owes money on student loans. Ben earns $40,000 a year at a part-time job, but he inherited a paid-off house and some savings from his grandparents. Who is better off? The answer depends on whether you look at income or wealth.

*Income* is the money that comes in over a period of time, such as wages, salary, rent from property, or interest from savings. *Wealth* is a snapshot of everything a person owns, such as a home, savings and stocks, minus everything they owe. Economists call wealth *net worth*. A person can have a high income but little wealth, or a small income but a lot of wealth.

The difference matters because wealth is usually shared much less evenly than income. In the United States, the Federal Reserve estimates that the richest tenth of households hold about two-thirds of all household wealth. The bottom half of households hold only a few percent. Wealth can also be passed down to children, so it helps explain why advantages can last across generations.

Wealth also acts as a cushion. A family with savings can survive a lost job or a medical bill. A family with no savings may have to borrow at high interest. Wealth can pay for college, a first home, or starting a business. That is why many researchers who study opportunity look closely at wealth, not just at paychecks.

words.d: money that comes in over a period of time, such as wages, salary or interest
the total value of what a person or family owns, minus what they owe
another name for wealth: assets minus debts

look.title: Who Holds U.S. Household Wealth

look.prompt: The bottom half of households is 50 percent of people. About what share of wealth does it hold, and what does that gap tell you?

check.q: Which of these is an example of wealth rather than income?
check.why: Wealth is what a person owns minus debts. A house is owned property, while paychecks, salary and tips are income.

choices: Ben owns an inherited house and savings
check.why: Ben earns less income, but he has more wealth because he inherited a paid-off house and savings.

check.q: According to the Federal Reserve estimate in the reading, the richest tenth of U.S. households hold about what share of wealth?
check.why: The reading says the richest tenth hold about two-thirds of household wealth, which shows how unequal wealth is.

lessons.title: The Gini Coefficient
lessons.mainIdea: The Gini coefficient is one number, from 0 to 1, that sums up how evenly income is shared in a country.
reading: Imagine a class of 30 students sharing 30 pizzas. If every student gets one pizza, the sharing is perfectly equal. If one student gets all 30 and everyone else gets nothing, the sharing is perfectly unequal. Real countries fall somewhere in between. Economists wanted one simple number to show where a country falls on that scale.

The most common tool is the *Gini coefficient*, named after the Italian statistician Corrado Gini, who described it in 1912. It runs from 0 to 1. A score of 0 means everyone has the same income. A score of 1 means one person has all of it. Many reports multiply the score by 100, so a Gini of 0.40 is often written as 40. Higher means more *inequality*, or a bigger gap.

The World Bank publishes Gini estimates for most countries. Nordic countries such as Norway, Denmark and Finland usually score in the mid to high 20s. The United States scores around 40. Latin America is often described as one of the most unequal regions, with Brazil and Colombia scoring above 50. South Africa has one of the highest scores measured anywhere, above 60.

A single number has limits. Two countries can have the same Gini but very different lives at the bottom. The Gini also says nothing about why a gap exists. Some measures use income before taxes, and others use income after taxes and government benefits. So careful readers always ask: which income, which year, and measured by whom?

words.d: a number from 0 (everyone equal) to 1 (one person has everything) that measures how evenly income is shared
a gap in how income, wealth or opportunity is shared among people
an expert who collects and studies numbers to find patterns

look.title: Income Gaps Around the World
look.cite: World Bank, Poverty and Inequality Platform, recent estimates (rounded; years differ by country)
look.prompt: Which country on this list has the most equal income sharing, and which has the least? How can you tell?

check.q: A country's Gini coefficient rises from 0.30 to 0.45. What does that mean?
check.why: A higher Gini means a bigger gap in how income is shared. It does not measure total wealth or population.

check.q: Which region does the reading describe as one of the most unequal in the world?
check.why: The reading says Latin America is often described as one of the most unequal regions, with Brazil and Colombia above 50.

check.q: What is one limit of the Gini coefficient named in the reading?
choices: It only works for Nordic countries
It does not explain why a gap exists
It cannot be written as a number
check.why: The reading says the Gini sums up the gap in one number but says nothing about its causes.

lessons.title: Poverty Lines and Living Standards
lessons.mainIdea: Poverty can be measured against a fixed line, like the World Bank's line for extreme poverty, or against what is normal in one country.
reading: A family in rural Malawi and a family in Chicago may both be called poor. Yet their lives are very different. The Malawi family may lack clean water and electricity. The Chicago family may have both but struggle to pay rent. To compare them, researchers need clear rules about what counts as poverty.

One rule is *absolute poverty*, which uses a fixed line that does not change from country to country. The World Bank sets an international line for *extreme poverty*. In 2022 it set that line at $2.15 per person per day, adjusted for prices in each country. Below that line, people struggle to afford enough food, shelter and basic care.

Another rule is *relative poverty*. Here, a person is poor if they have much less than most people in their own country. Many European countries count a household as poor if its income is below 60 percent of the middle income. Under this rule, a family in Norway could count as poor even though it lives far above the World Bank line.

Each measure answers a different question. Absolute lines ask whether people can meet basic needs. Relative lines ask whether people can take part in normal life where they live, like joining a school trip. Arguments about poverty often come down to which measure a speaker is using, so it helps to ask.

words.d: being below a fixed income line needed for basic needs, the same in every country
the World Bank's term for living below its lowest international poverty line
having much less income than most people in your own country

look.title: Two Kinds of Poor
look.text: Family A lives in a village with no electricity. The parents grow most of their own food, and in dry years the children eat once a day. Family B lives in a city apartment with heat and a phone. But after rent, there is little money for school clothes, and the children skip class trips because they cost too much.
look.prompt: Which family is in absolute poverty, and which fits relative poverty better? Explain using the terms.

check.q: Which measure would call a family poor because it earns much less than most families in its own country?
check.why: Relative poverty compares a family to others in the same country, such as below 60 percent of the middle income.

check.q: In 2022 the World Bank set its extreme poverty line at about how much per person per day?
check.why: The reading gives the World Bank's 2022 international extreme poverty line as $2.15 per person per day, adjusted for prices.

check.q: Why can a family in Norway count as poor under one measure but not another?
choices: It may be below Norway's relative line but far above the World Bank line
The World Bank does not measure Europe
check.why: Relative poverty compares to others in Norway, while the World Bank's absolute line is a fixed amount.

lessons.title: What Social Mobility Means
lessons.mainIdea: Social mobility is how easily people move up or down the ladder of income and status, especially compared with their parents.
reading: Picture a ladder with ten rungs. Everyone in a country stands on one rung, from the lowest incomes to the highest. Now picture the children of each person. Do the children end up on the same rung as their parents? Or do some climb higher and some slip lower? That movement is what *social mobility* means.

Researchers study two kinds. *Intergenerational mobility* compares children with their parents, such as a farmworker's daughter who becomes an engineer. Movement within one person's lifetime is called intra-generational mobility, like a cashier who becomes a store manager. Mobility can also be *absolute* or relative. Absolute mobility asks whether children earn more than their parents did at the same age. Relative mobility asks whether children change rungs compared with everyone else.

The economist Raj Chetty and his team studied tax records to measure absolute mobility in the United States. They found that about 90 percent of Americans born in 1940 grew up to earn more than their parents. For those born in 1980, it was about 50 percent. Slower economic growth and wider gaps both played a part, they argued.

High mobility is often seen as a sign of fairness. It suggests that talent and effort, not just family, shape where people end up. But people disagree about how much mobility is realistic and what helps it most. Some point to schools and neighborhoods. Others point to families, work and a growing economy.

words.d: movement of people up or down the ladder of income, education or status
how much children's position differs from their parents' position
whether children end up earning more than their parents did at the same age

look.title: Earning More Than Your Parents
look.cite: Chetty and others, "The Fading American Dream," Science, 2017 (rounded)
look.prompt: How did the chance of out-earning your parents change from 1940 to 1980? What might explain the drop?

check.q: A farmworker's daughter becomes an engineer. What kind of mobility is this?
check.why: Intergenerational mobility compares a child's position with her parents' position.

check.q: According to Chetty's research, about what share of Americans born in 1980 out-earned their parents?
check.why: The study found about 90 percent for those born in 1940 but only about 50 percent for those born in 1980.

check.q: What question does absolute mobility ask?
choices: Do children earn more than their parents did at the same age?
Do children change rungs compared with everyone else?
How equal is income in a country?
How much wealth does a family own?
check.why: Absolute mobility compares a child's earnings with the parents' earnings at the same age.

lessons.title: The Great Gatsby Curve
lessons.mainIdea: Economists describe a pattern called the Great Gatsby curve: countries with more inequality tend to have less mobility between generations.
reading: In the novel The Great Gatsby, published in 1925, a poor young man remakes himself as a rich one. But he never fully breaks into the old-money world he admires. In 2012 the economist Alan Krueger, then an adviser to the U.S. president, borrowed the book's title for a graph. The graph used research by the Canadian economist Miles Corak.

The graph places countries on two measures. One is income inequality, often measured by the Gini coefficient. The other is how closely children's earnings follow their parents' earnings. Economists call that second measure *earnings persistence*. When they drew the dots, a pattern appeared. Countries like Denmark and Norway had low inequality and low persistence. The United States and the United Kingdom had higher inequality and higher persistence.

This pattern is called the *Great Gatsby curve*. It is a *correlation*, meaning two things rise and fall together. A correlation does not prove that one causes the other. Supporters argue that big gaps let rich families buy advantages, such as better schools and tutors, which keeps children near their parents' rung.

Critics raise questions. Some say the countries differ in many ways, such as size, history and population, so the curve may mix up causes. Others say the data for some countries are weak. Still others argue that growth and strong families matter more than gaps. Economists still debate how much the curve tells us about cause.

words.d: a graph showing that countries with more income inequality tend to have less mobility between generations
a pattern where two things tend to change together, which does not by itself prove cause
how closely children's earnings follow their parents' earnings

look.title: Reading the Curve
look.text: Imagine a graph. Across the bottom is inequality, from low on the left to high on the right. Up the side is how much parents' earnings predict their children's earnings. Denmark and Norway sit near the lower left. The United States and the United Kingdom sit toward the upper right. Most other countries fall along a rising line between them.
look.prompt: What does the rising line suggest? Name one reason the line alone cannot prove that inequality causes low mobility.

check.q: Who named the Great Gatsby curve in 2012?
check.why: Alan Krueger named the curve in 2012, using research by Miles Corak.

check.q: Where do Denmark and Norway fall on the curve?
choices: Low inequality and low earnings persistence
High inequality and high earnings persistence
High inequality and low earnings persistence
check.why: The reading says the Nordic countries have low inequality, and children's earnings follow their parents' less closely.

check.q: Why do critics say the curve does not prove cause?
choices: It is a correlation, and countries differ in many other ways
check.why: A correlation shows two things moving together. Other differences between countries could explain the pattern.

lessons.title: Education as a Ladder
lessons.mainIdea: Education is one of the strongest ladders for moving up, but unequal schools can also pass advantages down.
reading: In 1862 President Abraham Lincoln signed the Morrill Act. It gave federal land to states to build public colleges. The University of Illinois grew from that law. For millions of students since then, a public college has been a step up. Education is often called a ladder because it can lift people whose parents never had the chance.

The numbers show why. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reports that workers with a bachelor's degree earn much more, on average, than workers with only a high school diploma. They are also less likely to be out of work. Economists call the extra pay for a degree the *college premium*. Skills and training are sometimes called *human capital*, because they work like an investment that pays off later.

But the ladder is not equal for everyone. In the United States, schools are partly paid for by local property taxes. Richer areas can often spend more per student. Families with more money can pay for tutors, test preparation and summer programs. So schooling can lift some students up while helping others stay ahead.

Countries try different fixes. Finland gives every school similar funding and trains all teachers to a high level. South Korea has intense exams, and many families pay for private after-school academies called hagwons. People argue about which approach helps most. Many agree that early childhood learning and strong teachers make a real difference.

words.d: the extra pay, on average, that workers with a college degree earn compared with those without one
the skills, knowledge and training a person has that help them earn a living
an 1862 U.S. law that gave land to states to build public colleges

look.title: What a Diploma Pays
look.cite: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, "Education pays," 2023 data (rounded)
look.prompt: About how much more per week does the typical worker with a bachelor's degree earn than one with a high school diploma?

check.q: What is the college premium?
choices: The extra average pay earned by workers with a degree
check.why: The college premium is the extra pay, on average, that degree holders earn compared with people without one.

check.q: How can U.S. schooling keep some advantages in place, according to the reading?
choices: All schools get the same money
Richer areas can spend more, and families can pay for tutors
The Morrill Act closed public colleges
check.why: Local property taxes and private spending on tutoring can give richer students extra help.

check.q: Which country is described as giving every school similar funding?
check.why: The reading says Finland gives schools similar funding and trains all teachers to a high level.

lessons.title: Class in Britain
lessons.mainIdea: In the United Kingdom, class has long been signaled by accent and schooling, and a small group from private schools still holds many top jobs.
reading: In Britain, people have often been able to guess each other's class within a few words. For generations, an accent called *Received Pronunciation* was linked to the upper and upper-middle class and to the BBC. Regional accents from Liverpool, Glasgow or East London were sometimes looked down on. Many working-class Britons are proud of their accents, and today the BBC hires presenters with many different ones.

Schools are another signal. In Britain, the oldest private schools, such as Eton and Harrow, are confusingly called public schools. Fees are high. The Sutton Trust, a charity that studies mobility, reports that only about 7 percent of British pupils attend private schools. Yet its 2019 study found that people from private schools held a much larger share of top jobs, such as senior judges.

The word *elite* means a small group at the top of a society. Critics argue that Britain's elite reproduces itself, with the same schools feeding the same universities, Oxford and Cambridge, and then the same jobs. Supporters of private schools reply that parents have a right to choose, and that the schools often give scholarships and share facilities.

Britain has also changed a great deal. After World War II, free secondary school and later new universities opened doors. Many prime ministers since then went to state schools. The debate today is about how fast the doors are opening, and what would open them wider.

words.d: a British accent long linked with the upper classes, schools like Eton and early BBC radio
a small group at the top of a society in wealth, power or status
in Britain, an old private fee-paying school such as Eton; in the U.S., a free government school

look.title: Private School and Top Jobs in Britain
look.cite: Sutton Trust and Social Mobility Commission, Elitist Britain, 2019 (rounded)
look.prompt: Compare the first row with the others. What pattern do you see, and what are two possible explanations?

check.q: In Britain, what does the term public school usually mean?
choices: A school run by the BBC
check.why: In Britain, old fee-paying schools like Eton are called public schools, unlike the American meaning.

check.q: According to the Sutton Trust, about what share of British pupils attend private schools?
check.why: The reading says only about 7 percent attend private schools, yet they hold a larger share of top jobs.

check.q: What argument do supporters of private schools make?

check.why: The reading says supporters stress parents' choice and point to scholarships and shared facilities.

lessons.title: India's Reservations Debate
lessons.mainIdea: India reserves places in colleges, government jobs and legislatures for groups that faced caste discrimination, and people still debate how the system should work.
reading: Dr. B. R. Ambedkar was born in 1891 into a caste that others treated as untouchable. As a boy, he was made to sit apart at school. He went on to earn doctorates in New York and London. After independence he led the committee that wrote India's Constitution, adopted in 1950. It banned untouchability and made room for the policy known as *reservations*.

Reservations set aside a share of seats in public colleges, government jobs and legislatures. At first they covered *Scheduled Castes*, the official name for groups once treated as untouchable, and Scheduled Tribes. In 1990 the government extended reservations to groups called Other Backward Classes, following the Mandal Commission report. In 1992 India's Supreme Court ruled that reservations should generally not go above 50 percent.

Supporters say reservations have opened doors for millions. They point to Dalit doctors, officers and members of Parliament whose families were once shut out. Dalit, meaning broken or oppressed, is a name many members of these communities chose for themselves. Supporters say caste bias still exists, so the help is still needed.

Critics raise other points. Some say benefits go mostly to better-off families within each group. Others argue that jobs should go by merit or by family income, not by caste. In 2019 India added a 10 percent reservation for poorer families outside the older groups. The debate continues in courts, colleges and elections.

words.d: India's policy of setting aside seats in colleges, jobs and legislatures for groups that faced discrimination
the official Indian name for caste groups once treated as untouchable
a name meaning broken or oppressed, chosen by many people from communities once treated as untouchable

look.title: Ambedkar on Political and Social Equality
look.text: Ambedkar warned that on January 26, 1950, India would enter a life of contradictions. In politics each person would have one vote and one value. But in social and economic life, deep inequality would remain. He argued that the country must remove this contradiction soon, or those who suffered from inequality would lose faith in democracy.
look.cite: B. R. Ambedkar, speech to the Constituent Assembly of India, November 25, 1949 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: What is the contradiction Ambedkar describes? How might reservations be one attempt to address it?

check.q: Who led the committee that wrote India's Constitution?
check.why: Ambedkar, born into a caste treated as untouchable, led the drafting committee for the 1950 Constitution.

check.q: What did India's Supreme Court rule in 1992 about reservations?
choices: They should generally not go above 50 percent
They apply only to private companies
They must cover 90 percent of seats
check.why: The reading says the 1992 ruling set a general limit of 50 percent.

check.q: What is one criticism of reservations named in the reading?
choices: They were never written into law
Benefits may go mostly to better-off families within each group
check.why: Some critics say the better-off families within reserved groups gain most of the benefits.

lessons.title: China's Great Climb
lessons.mainIdea: After reforms began in 1978, China's economy grew fast and hundreds of millions of people left extreme poverty, while new gaps also opened.
reading: In 1978, most people in China were farmers, and most were very poor. That year, a group of farmers in the village of Xiaogang secretly divided their collective land. Each family agreed to farm its own plot and keep what it grew above a quota. Their harvest jumped. Soon the government under Deng Xiaoping allowed this system across the country.

These changes were called *reform and opening*. Farmers could sell extra crops at market prices. In 1980 China created *special economic zones*, such as Shenzhen, where foreign companies could build factories. Shenzhen grew from a small town into one of the world's great cities. The Communist Party kept political control, but the economy became much more open to markets.

The results were huge. The World Bank estimates that close to 800 million people in China left extreme poverty from 1978 to about 2020. That is roughly three-quarters of the global drop in extreme poverty over those years. Millions moved from villages to cities to work in factories, building roads and shipping goods around the world.

The climb also brought new gaps. China's Gini rose, and coastal cities pulled ahead of inland villages. The *hukou* system, a household registration rule, often kept migrant workers from getting the same schools and health care as city-born residents. Some credit markets for the growth. Others credit the state's planning. Both sides study China closely.

words.d: China's economic changes after 1978 that allowed markets, private farming and foreign investment
an area with special rules to attract foreign companies and trade, such as Shenzhen
China's household registration system, which ties people's public services to their hometown

look.title: Two Readings of China's Growth
look.text: Economist A: China grew once it let farmers sell crops and let businesses compete. Markets and trade did the heavy lifting. Economist B: China grew because a strong state built roads, ports and power plants, and chose which industries to support. Markets alone would not have done it.
look.prompt: What evidence from the reading could each economist use? Which facts fit both views?

check.q: What did the farmers of Xiaogang do in 1978?
choices: They built a factory for foreign companies
They secretly divided collective land into family plots
check.why: The farmers divided their collective land so each family farmed its own plot, and harvests rose.

check.q: About how many people in China left extreme poverty from 1978 to about 2020, according to the World Bank?
check.why: The World Bank estimates close to 800 million people left extreme poverty in China over those years.

check.q: How did the hukou system create a gap?
choices: It often kept migrant workers from equal city schools and health care
It gave all land to foreign companies
check.why: Hukou ties services to a person's registered hometown, so many migrants in cities had fewer public services.

lessons.title: Explanations From Left and Right
lessons.mainIdea: People on the left and right often explain inequality differently, and each side points to real evidence.
reading: Two students watch the same news story about a closed factory in a small town. One says the company and the government let those workers down. The other says the town needs new businesses and workers need new skills. Both care about the workers. They just start from different ideas about what causes gaps and what fixes them.

Thinkers on the political *left* often stress *structural* causes. These are forces bigger than one person, such as unequal schools, discrimination, weak unions or tax rules that favor the rich. The philosopher John Rawls argued in 1971 that a fair society allows inequalities only if they help the worst-off. The left often supports higher taxes on the rich, stronger unions and public programs.

Thinkers on the political *right* often stress freedom, markets and personal responsibility. They argue that growth lifts most people, even if some rise faster. They point out that high taxes can weaken the reasons to work, save and invent. The economist Milton Friedman argued that putting equality ahead of freedom would harm both. The right often supports lower taxes, school choice and strong families.

Many people mix these views. Most agree that both personal choices and outside forces shape lives. The debate is about how much weight each deserves, and what a government should do. Good arguments on either side use evidence, like the data in this chapter.

words.d: caused by the way a whole society is set up, rather than by one person's choices
the side of politics that usually stresses equality and a larger role for government in reducing gaps
the side of politics that usually stresses freedom, markets, tradition and personal responsibility

look.title: Friedman on Equality and Freedom
look.text: Friedman argued that a society that puts equality of outcome ahead of freedom will end up with neither. A society that puts freedom first, he said, will end up with a great deal of both freedom and equality.
look.cite: Milton and Rose Friedman, Free to Choose, 1980 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Explain Friedman's claim in your own words. How might a follower of John Rawls answer him?

check.q: Which explanation of inequality is most typical of the political left?
choices: Growth lifts everyone, so gaps do not matter
Structural causes like unequal schools and weak unions
High taxes are the main cause of poverty
Personal choices are the only cause
check.why: The reading says the left often stresses structural causes that are bigger than one person.

check.q: What did John Rawls argue in 1971?
choices: Inequality is fair only if it helps the worst-off
check.why: Rawls argued that a fair society allows inequalities only when they benefit the worst-off.

check.q: What does the reading say most people actually do?
choices: Mix views, agreeing that choices and outside forces both matter
check.why: The reading says many people mix views and argue about how much weight each cause deserves.

lessons.title: Tools Countries Use
lessons.mainIdea: Countries use taxes, public services and growth policies to shape inequality and mobility, and each tool has supporters and critics.
reading: Norway taxes its citizens heavily and pays for free college, long paid parental leave and public health care. Singapore keeps many taxes low but requires workers to save part of every paycheck and builds public housing where most citizens live. Both countries are rich. They took different paths to share the gains.

One common tool is *redistribution*, moving money from richer to poorer through taxes and benefits. A *progressive tax* takes a higher percentage from higher incomes. In many European countries, taxes and benefits cut the Gini a great deal compared with income before taxes. Supporters say this protects families and gives children a fairer start. Critics say high taxes can slow growth and reduce the reward for effort.

Other tools focus on opportunity rather than outcomes. These include early childhood programs, job training and scholarships. Some focus on growth, such as lowering barriers to starting a business. Supporters on the right often argue that a growing economy creates more jobs and more chances to climb.

No country uses only one tool. Most mix taxes, public services and markets in different amounts. Voters in each country argue about the right mix. The best choice depends on what people value most, such as equality, freedom, security or growth, and on what the evidence shows works.

words.d: moving money from richer to poorer people through taxes and government benefits
a tax that takes a higher percentage from people with higher incomes
services paid for by government, such as schools, roads and health care

look.title: Design a Policy
look.text: Your town council has money for one new program. Option 1: free preschool for every four-year-old. Option 2: a tax cut for small businesses that hire local workers. Option 3: a cash payment to the lowest-income families each month.
look.prompt: Pick one option. Explain whether it mainly targets outcomes, opportunity or growth, and give one argument a critic might make.

check.q: What is a progressive tax?
choices: A tax everyone pays at the same rate
A tax that rises every year
A tax that takes a higher percentage from higher incomes
check.why: A progressive tax takes a larger share of income from people who earn more.

check.q: How does Singapore's approach differ from Norway's in the reading?
choices: Singapore keeps many taxes low but requires savings and builds public housing
Singapore taxes more heavily than Norway
Singapore has free college for all
check.why: The reading contrasts Norway's heavy taxes and services with Singapore's low taxes, required savings and public housing.

check.q: Which tool focuses on opportunity rather than outcomes?
check.why: The reading lists early childhood programs, training and scholarships as tools aimed at opportunity.

review.q: A retired teacher owns a paid-off home but lives on a small pension. She has:
review.why: Her pension is a small income, but her paid-off home is wealth.

review.q: Which country would most likely have the lowest Gini coefficient?
review.why: Nordic countries like Norway score in the mid to high 20s, among the most equal in the world.

review.q: What does the Great Gatsby curve show?
choices: Richer countries always have more mobility
More unequal countries tend to have less mobility between generations
review.why: The curve is a correlation: higher inequality tends to go with higher earnings persistence.

review.q: Which study found that about half of Americans born in 1980 out-earned their parents?
review.why: Chetty's team used tax records to measure absolute mobility in the United States.

review.q: How are India's reservations and Britain's debate about private schools alike?
choices: Both are about who gets access to top schools and jobs
Both were created by the World Bank
review.why: Both debates ask whether the paths to top schools and jobs are open fairly to all groups.

review.q: What began in China in 1978 under Deng Xiaoping?
review.why: China's reform and opening allowed family farming, markets and later special economic zones.

review.q: Which measure would call a family poor for earning far below the middle income in its own country?
review.why: Relative poverty compares a family with others in the same country.

review.q: A speaker says, "Unequal schools and weak unions hold people back." Which view is this closest to?
choices: A structural view often held on the left
A view that only markets matter
A view held only by the World Bank
review.why: Stressing forces bigger than one person, like schools and unions, is a structural view often linked with the left.

chapters.title: Culture, Migration and Identity
chapters.bigQuestion: When people and cultures move and mix, what is kept, what changes, and who decides?

story.title: Mole in Two Languages
story.kicker: In a Pilsen kitchen, a grandmother teaches a family recipe in Spanish, and her grandson answers in English.
paragraphs: On a Saturday morning in Pilsen, on Chicago's Lower West Side, Doña Rosa lays out dried chiles on her kitchen table. Ancho, mulato, pasilla. She came to Chicago from Michoacán, in Mexico, more than forty years ago. Today she is teaching her grandson Mateo how to make mole, the dark, rich sauce her mother made for every wedding and baptism.

"Primero, los tostamos, pero con cuidado," she says. First, we toast them, but carefully. Mateo is sixteen. He understands almost every word. But when he answers, it comes out in English. "Like this, Abuela? Not too long?" She nods and laughs. The two of them have talked this way his whole life, each in the language that feels most like home.

Outside, the neighborhood tells its own story. Murals of Mexican history cover the brick walls. Many of the old buildings were built by Czech immigrants more than a century ago. The name Pilsen itself comes from a city in what is now the Czech Republic. Down the street, a new coffee shop sells drinks at prices some longtime families find hard to pay.

As the sauce darkens, Mateo asks a question he has been thinking about. "If I make this for my kids someday, but I explain it in English, is it still our recipe?" His grandmother stirs for a long moment. "The recipe is in your hands," she says. "The words are in your heart. Use both."
story.think: What traditions in your family or community have changed as they were passed down? What stayed the same?

lessons.title: The Korean Wave and Anime
lessons.mainIdea: Popular culture from South Korea and Japan now reaches fans around the world, a sign of cultural globalization.
reading: In 2012 the South Korean singer Psy released "Gangnam Style." Its music video became the first on YouTube to pass one billion views. A few years later, the group BTS was filling stadiums in the United States and Brazil. In 2018 members of BTS spoke at the United Nations. Fans who did not speak Korean learned the words to their songs anyway.

This spread is often called the *Korean Wave*, or Hallyu. It began with Korean TV dramas that became popular across Asia in the late 1990s. The South Korean government and companies invested in music, film and games. In 2020 the Korean film Parasite became the first film not in English to win the Academy Award for Best Picture.

Japan's *anime*, or animated film and TV, followed a similar path. Studio Ghibli's Spirited Away won the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature in 2003. Series like Pokémon and Dragon Ball became favorites for children on every continent. Manga, the Japanese comics that many anime come from, now fill shelves in American libraries.

The spread of goods, ideas and culture across the world is called *globalization*. Some people worry it will make every place the same. But the Korean Wave shows a different pattern. Culture no longer flows only from the United States outward. Smaller countries can now reach huge audiences, and fans often learn about the place the culture came from.

words.d: the growing spread of goods, money, ideas and culture across the world
the worldwide spread of South Korean music, film and TV since the late 1990s, also called Hallyu
animated film and television from Japan

look.title: One Playlist, Many Places
look.text: A student in Chicago opens her music app. Her playlist has a BTS song from Seoul, a reggaeton hit from Puerto Rico, a theme song from a Japanese anime, and a song from a Bollywood film made in Mumbai. She has never visited any of those places.
look.prompt: What does her playlist show about globalization? Does it make cultures more alike, more different, or both? Explain.

check.q: What is the Korean Wave?
choices: The worldwide spread of South Korean pop culture
check.why: The Korean Wave, or Hallyu, is the spread of South Korean music, film and TV around the world.

check.q: Which film became the first not in English to win the Academy Award for Best Picture?
check.why: The reading says the Korean film Parasite won Best Picture in 2020.

check.q: What pattern does the Korean Wave show, according to the reading?
choices: Culture flows only from the United States
Only large countries can export culture
Culture now flows from many places, including smaller countries
check.why: The reading says culture no longer flows only from the United States, and smaller countries reach huge audiences.

lessons.title: Bollywood and Reggaeton
lessons.mainIdea: Bollywood films and reggaeton music show how a local style can grow from its roots into a global one.
reading: In Mumbai, India's largest city, film studios turn out hundreds of movies a year. This Hindi-language film industry is known as *Bollywood*, a blend of Bombay, the city's older name, and Hollywood. Bollywood films are famous for long stories, big family dramas and song-and-dance scenes. India as a whole makes more films each year than almost any other country.

Bollywood travels with the *diaspora*, the people of Indian heritage living around the world. Films open in London, Dubai, Toronto and Chicago. They are also popular in places with few Indian residents, such as parts of Africa and Central Asia. Many fans love the music and dancing even if they read the subtitles.

*Reggaeton* has a different story. It grew in Panama and Puerto Rico in the 1990s. It mixed Jamaican reggae and dancehall, hip-hop and Latin rhythms, with lyrics in Spanish. At first some radio stations would not play it. By 2017, "Despacito" by Luis Fonsi and Daddy Yankee became one of the most-streamed songs in history.

Both styles show *cultural hybridity*, the mixing of traditions into something new. Bollywood borrows from Indian classical dance and Hollywood musicals. Reggaeton borrows from Caribbean, African American and Latin music. In each case, the new style became a source of pride for the people who created it.

words.d: the Hindi-language film industry based in Mumbai, India
people living far from the homeland of their family or ancestors
a music style that grew in Panama and Puerto Rico in the 1990s, mixing reggae, hip-hop and Latin rhythms
the mixing of different cultural traditions into something new

look.title: Trace the Roots
look.text: A reggaeton song plays at a school dance. Its beat, called dembow, traces back to Jamaican dancehall. Its rhymes and flow echo hip-hop from New York. Its lyrics are in Puerto Rican Spanish. The dancers include students whose families come from Mexico, Poland, India and Nigeria.
look.prompt: List the cultures that shaped this one song. What does that list tell you about how new styles are born?

check.q: Where is Bollywood based?
check.why: Bollywood is the Hindi film industry in Mumbai, whose older name was Bombay.

check.q: Where did reggaeton grow in the 1990s?
check.why: The reading says reggaeton grew in Panama and Puerto Rico, mixing reggae, hip-hop and Latin rhythms.

check.q: What does cultural hybridity mean?
choices: Keeping a tradition exactly the same
check.why: Cultural hybridity is the blending of different traditions into a new style.

lessons.title: Food That Travels
lessons.mainIdea: Food is one of the oldest ways cultures spread, and dishes change as they move to new places.
reading: Order chicken tikka masala in London, and you are eating a dish many Britons call a national favorite. Its exact origin is debated, but it is widely linked to South Asian cooks in Britain. Order a California roll in Tokyo, and you may be eating sushi first made popular in North America. Food changes as it moves.

Food has always traveled. Chiles, tomatoes, corn and potatoes came from the Americas. After 1492 they spread to Europe, Africa and Asia in what historians call the *Columbian Exchange*. Before that, there were no chiles in Indian curry and no tomatoes in Italian sauce. Many dishes people think of as ancient are only a few centuries old.

Today, migrants carry food with them and open restaurants in new countries. Cooks often adjust recipes to local tastes and ingredients. This process is called *adaptation*. Chinese American dishes like General Tso's chicken are quite different from food in most of China. Tex-Mex food grew from Mexican cooking in Texas.

Some people say adapted dishes are less real. Others say adaptation is how food cultures have always stayed alive. Many immigrant cooks run two menus, one for newcomers and one for people from home. Food lets people share their culture with neighbors while keeping a taste of where they came from.

words.d: the transfer of plants, animals, people and diseases between the Americas and the rest of the world after 1492
changing something to fit a new place, such as adjusting a recipe to local tastes
a person who moves from one place to another to live or work

look.title: Where Did Your Lunch Come From?
look.text: A school lunch tray holds a slice of pizza with tomato sauce, a side of corn, a chocolate milk and an orange. Tomatoes, corn and cacao, the bean used to make chocolate, all first grew in the Americas. Oranges came from Asia. Wheat for the crust was first grown in the Middle East.
look.prompt: How many continents helped make this one lunch? What does that tell you about how old food exchange is?

check.q: What was the Columbian Exchange?
choices: The transfer of plants, animals and people between the Americas and the world after 1492
check.why: The Columbian Exchange began after 1492 and spread crops like tomatoes, corn and chiles around the world.

check.q: Which food first grew in the Americas?
check.why: The reading says tomatoes, corn, chiles and potatoes came from the Americas.

check.q: What is an example of adaptation in the reading?
choices: Growing wheat in the Middle East
General Tso's chicken in Chinese American restaurants
check.why: General Tso's chicken is a dish changed to fit American tastes, which is adaptation.

lessons.title: Why People Migrate
lessons.mainIdea: People migrate because of push factors that drive them away and pull factors that draw them to a new place.
reading: In 1990 a young nurse left Manila, in the Philippines, for a hospital job in New York. Her pay in the United States was many times higher, and she sent part of it home each month. Her story is one of millions. The United Nations estimates that about 281 million people lived outside the country they were born in by 2020.

Researchers sort causes into two kinds. *Push factors* drive people away, such as war, poverty, disasters or persecution. *Pull factors* draw them in, such as jobs, safety, schools or family already living there. Most people move for a mix of both. The largest sources of migrants today include India, Mexico, Russia and China.

A *refugee* is a person forced to flee their country because of war or persecution. International law, including a 1951 United Nations convention, gives refugees the right not to be sent back to danger. Other migrants move by choice to work or study. Many send money home. These payments, called *remittances*, are a major source of income for countries like Mexico, the Philippines and India.

Migration changes both places. Home countries can lose skilled workers but gain money and new ideas. New countries gain workers, businesses and culture. They also face questions about jobs, housing and how newcomers fit in. Those questions are at the center of the debates in the next lesson.

words.d: a reason that drives people to leave a place, such as war or poverty
a reason that draws people to a new place, such as jobs or safety
a person forced to flee their country because of war or persecution
money that migrants send back to family in their home country

look.title: Largest Countries of Origin for Migrants
look.prompt: Which country had the most people living abroad in 2020? What push or pull factors might explain it?

check.q: Which is a pull factor?
choices: A good job offer in another country
check.why: Pull factors draw people to a new place. A job offer is a pull; the others push people away.

check.q: What are remittances?
choices: Money migrants send to family back home
Papers needed to cross a border
check.why: Remittances are payments migrants send home, a major income source for countries like Mexico and the Philippines.

check.q: About how many people lived outside their birth country in 2020, according to the UN?
check.why: The United Nations estimate in the reading is about 281 million international migrants.

lessons.title: Assimilation, Multiculturalism, Integration
lessons.mainIdea: Countries choose different policies for newcomers, from assimilation to multiculturalism to integration, and each has supporters and critics.
reading: In 1908 a play called The Melting Pot opened in the United States. Its writer, Israel Zangwill, pictured immigrants blending into one new American people. That idea is called *assimilation*: newcomers adopt the language and customs of their new country and become part of the mainstream. Many American public schools once taught this goal directly.

Canada chose another path. In 1971 it became one of the first countries to adopt *multiculturalism* as official policy. The idea is that groups can keep their languages and traditions while being full citizens. Supporters often compare Canada to a mosaic, where each piece keeps its color. France, by contrast, stresses one shared republican identity and keeps religion out of public schools. A 2004 law bans conspicuous religious symbols there.

Many countries now speak of *integration*, a middle path. Newcomers learn the language and laws and take part in work and civic life. They may keep their culture at home and in their communities. Integration is described as two-way: newcomers adapt, and the country also adapts to them.

Each approach has critics. Some say assimilation erases heritage. Others say multiculturalism can leave groups living apart. In 2010 German Chancellor Angela Merkel said her country's attempt at multiculturalism had failed, and she called for more focus on learning German. Supporters of each model point to places where it has worked.

words.d: newcomers adopting the language and customs of a new country and blending into the mainstream
a policy that supports groups keeping their own cultures while being full citizens
a middle path where newcomers join common civic life while keeping parts of their culture

look.title: Melting Pot, Mosaic or Salad Bowl?
look.text: Person A: A country needs one shared language and shared values, or people will not trust each other. Person B: People should not have to give up their language or faith to belong. Person C: Newcomers should learn the language and laws, and the country should make room for their traditions too.
look.prompt: Match each person to assimilation, multiculturalism or integration. Which reasons does each give?

check.q: Which country adopted multiculturalism as official policy in 1971?
check.why: Canada became one of the first countries to make multiculturalism official policy in 1971.

check.q: Which idea did Israel Zangwill's 1908 play The Melting Pot express?
check.why: The melting pot pictures immigrants blending into one people, which is assimilation.

check.q: Why is integration called two-way?
choices: Newcomers adapt, and the country also adapts to them
People move in and then back out
It applies only to two countries
check.why: The reading says integration asks both newcomers and the country to adapt.

lessons.title: Debates About Migration
lessons.mainIdea: People disagree about how much migration a country should allow and how, and each side raises real concerns.
reading: In a town meeting, a factory owner says she cannot find enough workers and wants more visas. A retired machinist worries that newcomers will lower wages. A teacher says her classroom is richer for the students from many countries. A nurse points out that half the aides at her hospital were born abroad. Each speaker is describing something real.

Supporters of more migration often argue that newcomers fill jobs and start businesses. They say migrants pay taxes and help aging countries with too few young workers. Many also make a moral case: people fleeing danger deserve safety. Economists have found that migrants often start new companies at high rates.

People who want less or more controlled migration raise other concerns. Some worry about wages for workers without college degrees, pressure on housing and schools, or the speed of change in a neighborhood. Many stress the *rule of law*: that a country has the right to decide who enters and to enforce its rules. Economists disagree about how large the wage effects are.

These debates are about values as well as facts. How much should a country weigh the needs of newcomers against those of current residents? How fast can a community change and still hold together? Good arguments on any side use evidence and describe the other side fairly.

words.d: official permission to enter and stay in a country for a certain purpose and time
the idea that everyone, including the government, must follow the same laws
legal membership in a country, with its rights and duties

look.title: A Right to Leave
look.text: Everyone has the right to leave any country, including his own, and to return to his country.
look.cite: United Nations, Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 13, 1948
look.prompt: This article gives a right to leave a country. Does it say every country must let people in? Why might that difference matter in debates about migration?

check.q: Which argument is most often made by supporters of more migration?
choices: Countries have no right to borders
Newcomers fill jobs and help aging countries
check.why: The reading says supporters argue that newcomers fill jobs, pay taxes and help countries with too few young workers.

check.q: What does the rule of law mean in this debate?
choices: A country can decide who enters and must enforce its rules fairly
check.why: The rule of law means everyone follows the same laws, including a country's rules on who enters.

check.q: What does the reading say about wage effects of migration?
choices: Economists disagree about how large they are
check.why: The reading says economists disagree about the size of wage effects, so it is contested.

lessons.title: Saving Languages
lessons.mainIdea: Many of the world's languages are endangered, and communities are working to bring them back through schools and daily use.
reading: In 1982 a group of Māori elders in New Zealand opened small preschools called *kōhanga reo*, meaning language nests. Grandparents spoke only Māori to the toddlers all day. At that time, few Māori children spoke the language of their ancestors. Hundreds of language nests followed, then Māori-language schools. Today many more young Māori speak the language.

Experts count about 7,000 languages in the world. Groups that track them, such as Ethnologue and UNESCO, estimate that around 40 percent are *endangered*. An endangered language is one that children are no longer learning at home. When the last speakers pass away, a language becomes extinct, and with it go songs, stories and ways of seeing the world.

Languages often fade because of pressure from a bigger language used in schools, jobs and media. In the past, many governments punished children for speaking their home language at school. This happened in Indian boarding schools in the United States and in other countries. *Language revitalization* is the work of bringing a language back into daily life.

There are success stories. Hebrew was revived as an everyday spoken language in the late 1800s and 1900s. Welsh is taught in every school in Wales. In Paraguay, most people speak Guaraní, an Indigenous language that is official alongside Spanish. Each case shows that schools, families and pride can keep a language alive.

words.d: a language that children are no longer learning at home, so it may disappear
efforts to bring a fading language back into daily use
Māori-language preschools in New Zealand, meaning language nests

look.title: The Last Speaker
look.text: An elder is one of the last people who speaks her community's language fluently. She knows words for plants that are not in any dictionary, and songs sung only at harvest. Her grandchildren understand a little but answer in English. A local school asks her to teach one hour a week.
look.prompt: What would be lost if no one learned her language? What else, besides one hour a week, might help it survive?

check.q: What were the kōhanga reo?
check.why: Kōhanga reo were preschools opened in 1982 where elders spoke only Māori to young children.

check.q: About what share of the world's languages are endangered, according to experts in the reading?
check.why: The reading says groups like Ethnologue and UNESCO estimate around 40 percent of languages are endangered.

check.q: In which country is Guaraní, an Indigenous language, official alongside Spanish?
check.why: The reading says most people in Paraguay speak Guaraní, which is official with Spanish.

lessons.title: Indigenous Peoples Today
lessons.mainIdea: Indigenous peoples around the world are working to protect their lands, languages and self-government, with growing recognition of their rights.
reading: In northern Norway, the Sámi people have herded reindeer for centuries. In 1989 Norway opened a Sámi Parliament, an elected body that speaks for the Sámi on language, culture and land. Sweden and Finland have Sámi parliaments too. The Sámi still debate with governments about mines and wind farms on their traditional grazing lands.

*Indigenous peoples* are the descendants of the people who lived in a place before later settlers or states arrived. The United Nations estimates there are about 476 million Indigenous people in about 90 countries. They include Quechua communities in Peru, Māori in New Zealand, Ainu in Japan and hundreds of Native nations in the United States.

In 2007 the United Nations adopted the *Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples*. It affirms rights to culture, language and land, and to be consulted on projects that affect them. In the United States, there are over 570 federally recognized tribes. Each is a *sovereign nation* with its own government, which can run courts, schools and businesses.

Challenges remain. Many Indigenous communities face higher rates of poverty and fewer health services. Many also lead in protecting forests and rivers. Japan formally recognized the Ainu as an Indigenous people in a 2019 law. Change is often slow, but Indigenous leaders continue to shape it.

words.d: descendants of the people who lived in a place before later settlers or states arrived
a nation with its own government and the right to make many of its own decisions

words.w: Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples
words.d: a 2007 United Nations statement of Indigenous rights to culture, language, land and consultation

look.title: A Right to Be Consulted
look.text: The Declaration says states should consult and cooperate in good faith with Indigenous peoples through their own chosen representatives. They should seek their free and informed consent before approving projects that affect their lands, such as mines or dams.
look.cite: United Nations, Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, Article 32, 2007 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Think of the Sámi and a planned wind farm on grazing land. What would following this article require?

check.q: What did Norway open for the Sámi in 1989?
check.why: The reading says Norway opened a Sámi Parliament in 1989 to speak on language, culture and land.

check.q: What does it mean that U.S. tribes are sovereign nations?
choices: They have their own governments that can run courts, schools and businesses
check.why: Sovereign nations have their own governments and make many of their own decisions.

check.q: When did the UN adopt the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples?
check.why: The reading says the United Nations adopted the Declaration in 2007.

lessons.title: Exchange or Appropriation?
lessons.mainIdea: People argue about where cultural exchange ends and cultural appropriation begins, especially when sacred symbols or profit are involved.
reading: In 2012 the Navajo Nation sued a clothing company that sold items labeled "Navajo," including underwear and a flask. The Navajo Nation had registered its name as a trademark. It argued that the products used its name without permission and misled buyers. The case was settled in 2016. It sparked a wide debate about who can use a culture's name and symbols.

*Cultural exchange* is the sharing of ideas, arts and customs between groups, usually with respect and on both sides. It has always happened. *Cultural appropriation* is a term some people use when members of a more powerful group take elements of another culture without understanding, credit or permission. The concern is sharpest when the item is sacred, such as a feathered headdress worn in ceremonies.

People disagree about where the line falls. Some argue that borrowing is how culture grows, and that labeling it appropriation can discourage people from learning about others. Others argue that it matters who profits and who gets credit, especially for groups that were once punished for practicing their own culture.

Many people suggest a few questions to ask. Is the item sacred to the group? Does the group get credit or share the profit? Was it shared by members of that culture? Did I learn its meaning? These questions do not settle every case, but they help people think it through with respect.

words.d: respectful sharing of ideas, arts and customs between groups
a term for taking parts of another culture without understanding, credit or permission, often debated
a name or symbol registered by law so that only its owner can use it to sell goods

look.title: Three Cases
look.text: Case 1: A Korean grandmother teaches her neighbors to make kimchi, and they share it at a block party. Case 2: A company sells costume headdresses modeled on sacred ceremonial ones and keeps all the profit. Case 3: A Japanese chef opens a taco restaurant after training with cooks in Mexico City and names them on the menu.
look.prompt: Use the questions from the reading to decide which cases look like exchange and which might be called appropriation. Explain.

check.q: Why did the Navajo Nation sue a clothing company in 2012?
choices: The company used the Navajo name without permission
The company refused to sell Navajo art
check.why: The Navajo Nation held a trademark on its name and argued the company used it without permission.

check.q: When is the concern about appropriation sharpest, according to the reading?
choices: When food is shared at a party
When a recipe is taught in class
When the item is sacred, such as a ceremonial headdress
check.why: The reading says the concern is sharpest when sacred items are used without understanding or permission.

check.q: What is one argument against calling borrowing appropriation?
choices: Borrowing is how culture grows and it can encourage learning
check.why: Some argue that borrowing has always helped culture grow, and that the label can discourage learning about others.

lessons.title: Pilsen and Chinatown
lessons.mainIdea: Pilsen and Chinatown show how immigrant communities build neighborhoods that keep culture alive and change over time.
reading: Pilsen, on Chicago's Lower West Side, was first home to Czech immigrants in the late 1800s. They named it after Plzeň, a city in Bohemia. Many brick buildings and churches from that time still stand. Starting in the mid-1900s, Mexican families moved in, and Pilsen became one of the best-known Mexican American neighborhoods in the country.

Pilsen is famous for its murals, painted on walls, viaducts and schools. They show scenes from Mexican history, Aztec symbols and local leaders. The National Museum of Mexican Art, founded in 1982, is in Harrison Park. In recent years, rising rents and new businesses have brought *gentrification*. That means wealthier newcomers move in and costs rise, sometimes pushing out longtime residents.

A few miles east, Chicago's Chinatown centers on Cermak Road and Wentworth Avenue. Chinese immigrants moved there in the early 1900s from an older area downtown. The Chinatown Gate and the Pui Tak Center, with its green-and-red tile roof, are well-known landmarks. The neighborhood has grown with newer arrivals from mainland China, Hong Kong and Taiwan.

Both neighborhoods are examples of an *ethnic enclave*, an area where many people share a heritage. Enclaves give newcomers help with jobs, language and housing. Critics once worried they kept people apart. Many residents see them as a bridge, a home base for joining the wider city.

words.d: a neighborhood where many people share a heritage, with shops, churches and groups that serve them
a change where wealthier people move into a neighborhood, raising costs and sometimes pushing out longtime residents
a large painting on a wall or building

look.title: Walking 18th Street
look.text: Walk down 18th Street in Pilsen. You pass a panadería with trays of pan dulce, a mural of Mexican revolutionaries, a Catholic church built by Czech immigrants, a new coffee shop with pricey lattes, and a sign reading "Pilsen is not for sale."
look.prompt: What clues show the neighborhood's history? What clue shows a debate happening today, and what are the two sides?

check.q: Who first settled Pilsen and gave it its name?
check.why: Czech immigrants settled Pilsen in the late 1800s and named it after Plzeň in Bohemia.

check.q: What is gentrification?
choices: Wealthier newcomers moving in and raising costs
check.why: Gentrification means rising costs as wealthier people move in, sometimes pushing out longtime residents.

check.q: Where is the center of Chicago's Chinatown?
check.why: The reading says Chinatown centers on Cermak Road and Wentworth Avenue.

lessons.title: Devon Avenue and Ukrainian Village
lessons.mainIdea: Devon Avenue and Ukrainian Village show how many communities, faiths and generations can share and shape one city.
reading: On Devon Avenue, in the West Ridge neighborhood on Chicago's North Side, one block may hold a sari shop, a Pakistani restaurant and a Kosher bakery. Since the 1970s, many immigrants from India, Pakistan and Bangladesh have opened businesses there. Earlier, the area was home to a large Jewish community, which is still present. Some stretches of the street carry honorary names for Gandhi and for Muhammad Ali Jinnah, founder of Pakistan.

Devon Avenue shows *pluralism*, the idea that many groups with different faiths and backgrounds can live side by side as equals. Hindus, Muslims, Sikhs, Jews and Christians shop on the same street. India and Pakistan have a long and tense history. Yet here, their emigrants run businesses next to each other and serve each other's families.

Ukrainian Village, west of downtown, grew in the early 1900s as Ukrainian immigrants arrived. The golden domes of St. Nicholas Ukrainian Catholic Cathedral rise over the neighborhood. The Ukrainian National Museum and churches keep traditions alive, such as pysanky, eggs decorated with wax and dye for Easter.

Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the neighborhood has held rallies and collected aid. Longtime families have also welcomed new arrivals fleeing the war. The neighborhood has changed too, with many young residents of every background. Chicago's neighborhoods show that *identity* can be both deeply rooted and open to change.

words.d: the idea that many groups with different faiths and backgrounds can live together as equals
a person's sense of who they are, shaped by family, culture, faith, language and experience
Ukrainian Easter eggs decorated with wax and dye in detailed patterns

look.title: Mapping Your Identity
look.text: Mateo, from the chapter story, draws a map of his identity. At the center: Mexican American and Chicagoan. Around it: Spanish at home, English at school, Catholic, soccer fan, K-pop listener, grandson of a cook from Michoacán, friend of a classmate whose family runs a shop on Devon Avenue.
look.prompt: Which parts of Mateo's identity come from family, and which from the wider city? Sketch or list your own identity map.

check.q: What does pluralism mean?
choices: Many groups living together as equals
check.why: Pluralism is the idea that different faiths and backgrounds can live side by side as equals, as on Devon Avenue.

check.q: Which communities are described on Devon Avenue?
choices: South Asian businesses alongside a long-standing Jewish community
check.why: The reading says immigrants from India, Pakistan and Bangladesh share Devon Avenue with a Jewish community.

check.q: How has Ukrainian Village responded since 2022?
choices: It held rallies, collected aid and welcomed new arrivals
check.why: The reading says the neighborhood held rallies, collected aid and welcomed people fleeing the war.

review.q: Which is the best example of globalization of culture?
choices: A town that bans foreign films
Fans in Brazil singing BTS songs in Korean
review.why: Globalization is the spread of culture across borders, like Korean pop music reaching Brazil.

review.q: How are reggaeton and Bollywood alike?
choices: Both are sung only in English
Both grew from local roots into global styles by mixing traditions
review.why: Each is an example of cultural hybridity that grew from a local scene to a world audience.

review.q: A family leaves home because of war. The war is a:
review.why: Push factors drive people away, and war is a leading example.

review.q: Which policy asks newcomers to blend into one mainstream culture?
review.why: Assimilation, pictured as a melting pot, asks newcomers to adopt the main culture.

review.q: The kōhanga reo in New Zealand and Welsh in every school in Wales are both examples of:
review.why: Both are efforts to bring a fading language back into daily use.

review.q: Which is a right affirmed by the 2007 UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples?
choices: The right to leave any country
The right to a college degree
The right to be consulted on projects that affect their lands
review.why: The Declaration affirms rights to culture, language and land, and to be consulted on projects.

review.q: Which Chicago neighborhood was named after a city in Bohemia?
review.why: Czech immigrants named Pilsen after Plzeň, a city in Bohemia.

review.q: What question can help decide whether a use of culture is exchange or appropriation?
choices: Is the item sacred, and does the group get credit?
review.why: The reading suggests asking whether an item is sacred and whether its group gets credit or shares profit.
